p35: 35.  The Explanatory Report on the 1980 Hague Convention on International Child Abduction, drawn up by Elisa Pérez-Vera and published by the Hague Conference on Private International Law (HCCH) in 1982, is intended to highlight the principles which form the basis of the Hague Convention and to provide a detailed commentary on its provisions to those who are responsible for applying it. It is apparent from that report that, in order to discourage the possibility for the abductor to have his or her action legalised in the State of refuge, the Convention enshrines, in addition to its preventive aspect, the restoration of the status quo by means of an order for the immediate return of the child, which allows the situation that has been unilaterally and unlawfully altered to be restored. Compliance with custody rights falls almost entirely outside the scope of the Convention, since this matter must be discussed before the competent courts of the State where the child had his or her habitual residence prior to removal. The philosophy of the Hague Convention is to fight the increase in international child abductions, always being inspired by a desire to protect children and acting as interpreter of their true interests. Accordingly, the objectives of prevention and immediate return correspond to a specific conception of “the best interests of the child”. However, since the removal of a child may be justified by objective reasons relating either to the child’s person or to the environment with which he or she is most closely connected, the Convention recognises certain exceptions to the general obligation assumed by States to secure the immediate return of children (§ 25). Since the return of the child is the basic principle of the Convention, the exceptions to the general obligation to secure it form an important aspect in understanding the exact extent of that obligation, and it is possible to distinguish exceptions based on three different justifications (§ 27). Firstly, the authorities of the requested State are not bound to order the return of the child where the applicant was not actually exercising custody rights or where his or her behaviour shows acceptance of the new situation (§ 28). Secondly, Article 13, paragraph 1 (b) and paragraph 2, contain exceptions which clearly derive from a consideration of the interests of the child, to which the Convention gives a definite content. Thus, the interest of the child in not being removed from his or her habitual residence without sufficient guarantees of stability in the new environment gives way before the primary interest of any person in not being exposed to physical or psychological danger or being placed in an intolerable situation (§ 29). Lastly, there is no obligation to return a child where, in terms of Article 20, his or her return “would not be permitted by the fundamental principles of the requested State relating to the protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms” (§ 31). The Explanatory Report, which elaborates on those exceptions, also emphasises the margin of appreciation inherent in the judicial function.
p36: 36.  In 2003 the HCCH published the “Guide to Good Practice under the Hague Convention of 25 October 1980 on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction – Part II”. Although primarily intended for new Contracting States and having no binding effect, especially in respect of the judiciary, that document seeks to facilitate the implementation of the Convention by providing numerous recommendations and clarifications. It repeatedly emphasises the importance of the Explanatory Report on the Hague Convention, known as the Pérez-Vera Report, in assisting with the consistent interpretation and understanding of the Hague Convention (see, for example, point 3.3.2 “Implications of the transformation approach” and point 8.1 “Explanatory Report on the Convention: the Pérez-Vera Report”). It places particular emphasis on the fact that judicial and administrative authorities are under an obligation, among other things, to process return applications expeditiously, including on appeal (point 1.5 “Expeditious procedures”). Expeditious procedures should be viewed as procedures which are both fast and efficient: prompt decision-making under the Convention serves the best interests of children (point 6.4 “Case management”). The Guide to Good Practice specifies that delay in enforcement or non-enforcement of return orders in certain Contracting States are matters of serious concern, and recommends that Contracting States ensure that there are simple and effective mechanisms to enforce orders for the return of children, noting that the return must actually be effected and not merely ordered (point 6.7 “Enforcement”).
